algorithm: READ THE ASK FIRST. Read the question line before the scenario: is it FIRST, BEST, MOST likely cause, LEAST risk, or select N? Note the response count before you read a single option.

CIRCLE THE BINDING CONSTRAINT. Name the one constraint that decides the item (irreversibility, regulation, p95 at peak, audience, lifecycle stage, reach across machines, cost ceiling) and mark the trigger words. Also mark what the stem says is unchanged or already true.

CLASSIFY THE QUESTION. Does it want prevention or detection? Which layer did the triggering change touch? Which lifecycle stage are you in? Which ladder applies (pattern, control, HITL, integration, retrieval, diagnosis, lever, SLA, eval, lifecycle, reach)? Walk that ladder and stop at the lowest rung that satisfies the constraint.

STRIKE BY TRAP CODE. For each option, name the trap it matches (T-REMOVE, T-ENFORCE, T-LAYER, T-LATER and so on) and cross it out. An option you cannot pin to a trap stays in play. Good practice that ignores the binding constraint is still a trap.

TIE-BREAK ON ASSUMPTIONS. For the last two options, ask what each one needs to be true. The wrong one relies on a fact the stem never gave (T-ASSUME). If both hold up, take the one that fixes the cause rather than a symptom, at the strongest sufficient control or the simplest sufficient pattern.
RECOUNT AND COMMIT. Check that you picked exactly N options and that each one changes the outcome. Flag anything past 3 minutes and move on. Never leave an item blank.

laws.text: Find the binding constraint first; it decides between two good answers.
laws.why: Most distractors are sound practice. The constraint the stem states (irreversibility, regulation, p95 at peak, audience, stage) is what separates the answers, and a legal or SLA gate eliminates options outright rather than being weighed.

laws.text: Remove, don't guard. If the role never needs a capability, take it away.
laws.why: A capability that is gone cannot misfire or be injected into. Confirmation prompts, logging and time windows are compensating controls, and they leave the blast radius where it was.

laws.text: A prompt is not a guarantee. When it must hold every time, enforce it in code.
laws.why: Instructions, CLAUDE.md and bold text only make compliance more likely. Ask what physically stops the outcome if the model ignores the instruction: tool removal, permission rules, a fail-closed hook, app-layer authorization, schema validation or a workflow gate.

laws.text: Choose the simplest pattern that is sufficient, and pay only for variability the stem shows.
laws.why: Every step up in autonomy adds cost, latency and failure surface. If nothing varies between two requests, use a workflow. If one augmented call does the job, both the workflow and agent answers are wrong.

laws.text: Diagnose the layer the change touched, and look at traces before you fix anything.
laws.why: The variables the stem calls unchanged let you eliminate options. Start at the triggering change and compare traces of failing and passing runs. Swapping models, widening access or failing over first hides the evidence. Exception: when users are being actively harmed and a known-good version exists (a recent release), contain first by rolling back behind the flag or using a kill switch, then diagnose from the traces already captured (CS-D4-19).

laws.text: Measure the dominant term before you pull a cost or latency lever.
laws.why: Caching, batching, tier routing, trimming and streaming each fix a different term. The wrong lever either does nothing or quietly breaks the accuracy floor. Streaming changes perceived wait, not completion time.

laws.text: A number without a threshold is not an eval. Fix the metric, threshold, slices and stopping rule in advance.
laws.why: A threshold chosen after the results is a story, not a test. Judges must be calibrated against human labels, eval sets must stay held-out and fresh, and every subgroup must clear the bar on its own.

laws.text: Bring the evidence to the decision owner, framed for that audience. Do not decide for them or promise certainty.
laws.why: The architect owns an honest trade-off framing. The accountable stakeholder owns the decision. Quietly redefining the bar, abandoning it, bypassing the owner or offering guarantees all fail the Professional standard.

multi_rules: Read the select-N count before the options, and pick exactly N. Treat each item as all-or-nothing: the official guide says only that each item states how many to select, and the no-partial-credit claim comes from the community.
Judge every option on its own against the binding constraint. Keep only the options that change the outcome the stem asks about. An option that is merely true or harmless does not count.
The filler (T-FILLER) is the next-most-reasonable good practice: documentation, training, a dashboard or more logging that would not change the result. Drop it even though it sounds responsible.

Look for complementary pairs. The right answers often combine a preventive with a detective control, a technical fix with a stakeholder action, or a control with its evidence artefact. Two options that do the same job are rarely both correct.

Two rungs of the same ladder that substitute for each other (for example 'add a confirmation step' and 'remove the tool', where removal makes the confirmation moot) are alternatives. At most one is right, so take the strongest sufficient rung. Layers that each catch what the other misses (an output guardrail plus a mandatory approval before an external send) are complementary, and both can be right when the stem asks only for prevention.
Also strike options that belong to a later lifecycle stage (T-LATER) or that are right only under an assumption the stem never gave (T-ASSUME). Do not use them to pad your count to N.

rows.signal: Sponsor asks for 'a chatbot'; pain point never quantified
rows.choose: Reframe to the underlying job; agree baseline, target, constraints, owner first
rows.not: Prototype the chatbot or pick a model straight away
rows.unless: Baseline, target, constraints and owner are already agreed, and the stem asks for the build step.
rows.rule: Before you choose any pattern, model or price, restate the request as the job to be done. Then agree the baseline, target, constraints and decision owner.

rows.signal: Headline accuracy percentage offered as proof the design works
rows.choose: Convert to errors per period; ask which cases fail and their cost
rows.not: Accept the aggregate rate as the success measure
rows.rule: Convert an accuracy rate into an error count at real volume. Which cases fail, and what each failure costs, decides the architecture.

rows.signal: Design ends at output; quality 'watched on a dashboard'
rows.choose: Close the loop: capture outcomes and corrections, route to a named owner, feed evals
rows.not: A dashboard or log alone as the feedback stage
rows.rule: A design is end-to-end only when real outcomes flow back to a named owner who acts on them. A dashboard nobody owns is an open loop.

rows.signal: Answers must reflect current stock, balances or order status
rows.choose: Tool call to the system of record at request time
rows.not: Re-index or re-embed the live data more often
rows.unless: Slow-changing reference knowledge (policies, manuals) belongs in retrieval (or, when small and stable, well under ~200k tokens, a cached prompt prefix with no RAG), not a live call.
rows.rule: Fetch live state from the system of record at request time. Retrieval indexes are for knowledge that changes slowly.

rows.signal: Legacy caller times out after a few seconds, synchronously
rows.choose: Go async: return a job ID now, deliver by callback or polling
rows.not: Downsize the model or trim context to beat the timeout
rows.rule: If the caller's timeout is shorter than the work, change how the call works (an async job plus a callback) rather than cutting the quality of the work.

rows.signal: Fixed document structure; every step must be auditable
rows.choose: Workflow: code-defined steps, validation gates, logged intermediate outputs
rows.not: Autonomous agent because the task is complex
rows.unless: The steps cannot be listed in advance AND an occasional unexpected output is acceptable and recoverable. Then an agent is justified.
rows.rule: Choose the simplest pattern that works. One step is an augmented call. A path known in advance is a workflow. Only a path that emerges at runtime, with recoverable errors, earns an agent.

rows.signal: 'Just' answer staff policy questions from our documents
rows.choose: One augmented LLM call: retrieve, answer grounded, cite; no loop
rows.not: Build a multi-step workflow or agent loop
rows.unless: The job has several dependent stages that need separate checks, or a path that emerges at runtime. Then move up to a workflow or an agent.
rows.rule: If one call with retrieval or tools meets the requirement, both the workflow answer and the agent answer are over-engineering.

rows.signal: Eligibility or payout must be identical every time; auditors check
rows.choose: Deterministic code owns rules and calculations; Claude interprets unstructured input only
rows.not: Stricter prompt wording or a larger model for consistency
rows.rule: Anything that must come out the same every time, or that regulation requires, is enforced in deterministic components outside the model.

rows.signal: One agent per department, 'to match who owns it'
rows.choose: Split only for real independence or irreconcilable specialisation; else one agent
rows.not: Mirror the org chart with an agent per team
rows.unless: The subtasks are truly independent and can run in parallel (breadth-first research). Then orchestrator-workers with subagents is right.
rows.rule: Add a second agent only for real independence or specialisation that cannot be reconciled. Team structure is never evidence. Splitting costs you guaranteed ordering, halt-on-failure and a single audit trail.

rows.signal: Subagent output ignores constraints the coordinator already knew
rows.choose: Pass goal, constraints, required facts and output schema explicitly in handoff
rows.not: Assume the subagent sees the coordinator's history
rows.unless: A standing rule that every agent needs (a repo convention) can live in CLAUDE.md, which Claude Code subagents load. Task-specific facts still go in the handoff.
rows.rule: A subagent starts in a fresh context and sees none of the coordinator's conversation, findings or task constraints (only a Claude Code fork inherits the history); in Claude Code it does load the CLAUDE.md hierarchy and inherit tools and permissions. Every handoff must carry the goal, constraints, facts and return format the subagent needs.

rows.signal: One long prompt covers many aspects; sections skipped or shallow
rows.choose: Decompose: section independent parts, chain dependent ones, then synthesise
rows.not: Bigger window, more context or stronger model, same single prompt
rows.rule: Structural defects (missed coverage, a lost middle, shallow sections) need decomposition by dependency and independence. More volume or a bigger model does not fix them.

rows.signal: Each step needs the previous output; stop if a check fails
rows.choose: Prompt chain with programmatic gates; one orchestrator owns sequencing
rows.not: Parallel peer agents coordinating handoffs among themselves
rows.unless: The subtasks only become known after the input is inspected. Then use orchestrator-workers, where the model decides the split.
rows.rule: Chain dependent steps with gates in code, and run independent steps in parallel sections. Use a model-decided split only when the split cannot be known until runtime.

rows.signal: Faster per case, yet the deck claims 'transformation'
rows.choose: Name pillar by denominator: per unit efficiency, per person productivity, new transformation
rows.not: Relabel a faster existing process as transformation
rows.rule: Name the value pillar by its denominator. Gains per unit of work are efficiency, gains per person are productivity, and work that was not possible before is transformation. Removing a role counts as efficiency.

rows.signal: Cheapest design misses the p95-at-peak SLA but tops the weighted scorecard
rows.choose: Eliminate options that miss the SLA before scoring cost or preference
rows.not: Trade the SLA miss against savings in a weighted score
rows.rule: Performance SLAs are gates, not weights: drop any option that misses p95 at peak before cost or preference is compared.

rows.signal: Six teams call the model API directly with their own keys; no shared budget, logging or pinning
rows.choose: Route every call through one gateway: central auth, quotas and budgets, logging, routing, version pinning
rows.not: Ask each team to add logging and budget alerts to its own integration
rows.unless: One team, one app and one provider. Controls in that app's own code are then simpler than a gateway.
rows.rule: When many teams or apps call the model, put one gateway in the path so that authentication, budgets, logging, routing, version pinning and redaction apply to every call, with the provider behind an adapter.

rows.signal: Agent retried a refund tool call after a timeout; some customers were refunded twice
rows.choose: Make the side effect idempotent: an idempotency key per action, checked by the handler before acting
rows.not: Tell the agent in the prompt never to retry a refund
rows.unless: The action is naturally idempotent (a read, or setting a field to a fixed value). A plain bounded retry is then safe.
rows.rule: A retried side effect must not act twice. Give each state-changing tool call an idempotency key that the handler checks, and retry only transient errors, with jittered backoff and a cap.

rows.signal: Synthesis report silently omits sections whenever a worker times out
rows.choose: Orchestrator reconciles results against units dispatched; bounded retry per worker; explicit gap flags
rows.not: Ask the synthesis step to mention anything that seems to be missing
rows.rule: In a fan-out the orchestrator owns failure: it bounds retries per worker, requires explicit gap flags and checks returned results against dispatched units before synthesis.

rows.signal: Billing, outage and legal-threat messages share one prompt; each class is handled poorly
rows.choose: Routing: classify first; each class gets its own prompt, tools or tier; human-only class goes to a queue
rows.not: Keep one prompt and add a section for every message class
rows.unless: The classes need the same handling and one prompt already clears the bar on every slice.
rows.rule: When input classes need different handling, classify first (with a cheap tier or code) and route each class to its own prompt, schema, tools or tier; classes only a person may handle go to a queue.

rows.signal: Drafts must meet a written checklist; first drafts often miss an item
rows.choose: Evaluator-optimizer: generate, critique against the checklist, revise; retry cap, then escalate
rows.not: An autonomous agent that decides its own steps and when it is done
rows.unless: The criteria are vague or feedback does not measurably improve drafts. The loop then adds cost without quality, so fix the criteria first.
rows.rule: Use a generate-critique loop only when the evaluation criteria are clear and feedback measurably improves the output. Cap the retries, check in code whatever code can check, and escalate what still fails.

rows.signal: Twelve candidate use cases; the sponsor asks which to build first
rows.choose: Score each on quantified value, feasibility (data readiness, rights) and risk; start high value, feasible, low risk
rows.not: Prototype the most exciting idea to build momentum
rows.unless: A hard obligation or deadline forces one use case regardless of score. That gate then decides first.
rows.rule: Rank candidate use cases on quantified value, feasibility and risk, and start where value is high and feasibility and risk are favourable. SLA gates eliminate designs for one system; they do not rank use cases.

rows.signal: High-volume ticket triage; flagship everywhere; budget ceiling cut
rows.choose: Cheapest tier clearing the eval bar; route hard slice upward
rows.not: Flagship tier on every request to be safe
rows.rule: Pick the cheapest tier that clears an eval bar agreed in advance on your own traffic, send only the measured hard slice to a higher tier, and keep measuring after launch.
rows.unless: Volume is low and a single error is very costly. Starting on the top tier can then be the proportionate choice.

rows.signal: Errors only on multi-step reasoning cases; retrieval verified correct
rows.choose: Give that slice step-by-step reasoning or a higher effort setting first; if it still misses the bar, route only that slice to a higher tier; re-evaluate
rows.not: Keep cheapest tier regardless of fit to protect budget
rows.rule: A higher tier is justified only when measured failures come down to reasoning depth after prompt and retrieval are ruled out, and only for that slice.
rows.unless: Failures are spread evenly across case types. That points to the prompt, not the tier.

rows.signal: p95 latency over budget; traces show output tokens dominate
rows.choose: Cap and template the output, lower reasoning effort, then re-check the eval bar
rows.not: Trim input context, the term that does not dominate
rows.rule: When output tokens dominate latency, shorten the output (caps, templates, lower effort) and confirm the eval bar still holds before you change tier. Levers aimed at input do not move this term.
rows.unless: Output is already minimal and a faster tier is measured to clear the bar on this traffic. Switching tier is then the lever.

rows.signal: 'Must never' quote above policy limit or skip ID check
rows.choose: Enforce in code: tool precondition, validation gate, or remove capability
rows.not: Stronger system prompt wording, bold rules, more examples
rows.rule: A system prompt shapes behaviour only probabilistically. Anything that must hold every time (money, identity, compliance, safety ordering) is enforced by code outside the model, and the prompt only explains the rule.
rows.unless: The requirement is tone, style or preference and occasional deviation is acceptable. The prompt is then the right home. For a semantic content-scope rule (topics to avoid in open chat) with no deterministic check point, the system prompt is the primary control, backed by a separate classifier screen; a keyword filter alone is not enforcement.

rows.signal: Select TWO guardrails: customer account numbers reaching the model
rows.choose: Tokenise before the call (prevent) plus output scan with alerting (detect)
rows.not: Tell the model to ignore PII; redact responses afterward
rows.rule: Guardrails come in pairs: a preventive control placed before data crosses the boundary, and a detective control that catches what slips through. A prompt instruction or after-the-fact redaction is neither.

rows.signal: Report sections and tone vary run to run; content correct
rows.choose: Add a few complete worked examples covering the ambiguous cases
rows.not: Upgrade tier or add chain-of-thought
rows.rule: Match the technique to the failure. Zero-shot is the default while it clears the bar, few-shot examples fix format, tone and structure, and step-by-step reasoning fixes multi-step logic.
rows.unless: If output must be machine-valid every time, add a schema or tool contract plus validation. If zero-shot already clears the bar, adding examples would anchor varied inputs to one pattern.

rows.signal: Multi-step pricing math wrong; format and retrieval fine
rows.choose: Stepwise reasoning before the answer; exact arithmetic via a code tool
rows.not: Add more format examples or retrieved context
rows.rule: Reasoning errors call for structured step-by-step reasoning, and exact calculation belongs in a deterministic tool. More examples or more context do not repair logic.
rows.unless: The task is simple single-label classification. Chain-of-thought then adds tokens and latency without improving accuracy, so stay zero-shot.

rows.signal: Cost rising and mid-context facts missed on large inputs
rows.choose: Reduce what enters: relevance-filter inputs, clear stale tool results
rows.not: Bigger window, reorder sections, or 'read carefully'
rows.rule: Context is a finite budget. When cost and recall get worse together the cause is volume, so cut what enters the window (relevance filtering, clearing tool results, structured facts from upstream steps) instead of enlarging, reordering or adding emphasis.
rows.unless: The facts being dropped are ones the task needs. Restructure or retrieve more precisely instead; never cut required context. A single buried instruction at normal volume is a placement problem: move it after the long material (CS-D2-13).

rows.signal: Long agent session nearing limit; earlier decisions must survive
rows.choose: Compact to a structured summary keeping decisions, open state, next steps
rows.not: Truncate the oldest turns to fit
rows.rule: In long sessions, summarise the state you still need (compaction with complete instructions) and clear what is stale. Blind truncation silently drops context the task still requires.
rows.unless: The oldest content is used-up tool output that nothing needs. Clearing it outright is correct.

rows.signal: Same large system prompt and policy sent every request
rows.choose: Static prompt and policy first, dynamic input last; enable caching
rows.not: Truncate policy, downsize regardless of fit, or move to few-shot
rows.rule: When a large, stable prefix repeats across requests, put stable content first and cache it. It is the lever that cuts both time-to-first-token and input cost without dropping required context.
rows.unless: Cost is mostly output tokens, or the prefix is rarely reused within the cache lifetime. Measure before expecting savings; caching also leaves window occupancy unchanged.

rows.signal: Caching enabled but hit rate near zero
rows.choose: Find first changing byte; move timestamps and IDs after breakpoint
rows.not: Lengthen cache lifetime or add more breakpoints
rows.rule: Any change early in the prefix (a timestamp, a user ID, reordered tools, shuffled documents, an edited Skill list) invalidates everything after it. Find the first difference and move volatile values after the cached prefix.
rows.unless: The prefix is stable but requests arrive further apart than the default five-minute lifetime and within an hour. The 1-hour cache lifetime is then the fix.

rows.signal: Review procedure copied into five teams' prompts, drifting; fetches nothing
rows.choose: Versioned Skill or shared template module: owned, eval-gated, version-pinned
rows.not: Wrap the know-how in a new MCP server
rows.rule: Reusable know-how that needs no live data becomes a Skill or template module that is versioned, owned and gated by evals. MCP is for capabilities that must reach another system at runtime.
rows.unless: Several clients need live access to an external system. An MCP server is then the right way to reuse it.

rows.signal: One critical instruction in a long prompt is ignored; input volume is normal
rows.choose: Put long material first, the instruction and query last; delimit each part with XML tags
rows.not: Repeat the rule in capitals and bold it
rows.unless: The rule must hold every time. Then enforce it in code; placement only makes compliance more likely.
rows.rule: When one rule in a long prompt is missed and volume is not the problem, fix placement and separation: long material at the top, the instruction and query at the end, each part in its own tag.

rows.signal: Stakeholder proposes fine-tuning Claude on the policy manual so it knows current rules
rows.choose: Retrieval or a cached prompt for changing knowledge; prompts, examples and templates for behaviour
rows.not: Fine-tune the model on the manual and retrain whenever policy changes
rows.unless: A narrow, stable behaviour still fails after prompting and examples are exhausted, the platform offers fine-tuning for the chosen model, and evals show the gain.
rows.rule: Exhaust prompting, examples and retrieval before fine-tuning. Changing knowledge belongs in retrieval or tools, and Claude fine-tuning availability is limited, so an option that depends on it assumes a fact the stem rarely grants.

rows.signal: Staff only read and draft; agent also holds refund and delete
rows.choose: Remove the refund and delete tools from this role's toolset
rows.not: Keep them behind confirmation prompts, audit logs or business hours
rows.rule: Least privilege means removing the capabilities a role does not need. Logging, confirmation steps and time windows are only compensating or detective controls (official Sample 1).
rows.unless: The role genuinely needs the action. Then scope it narrowly and gate it by reversibility and blast radius.

rows.signal: Wrong-tool picks rising as one agent's catalogue keeps growing
rows.choose: Scope toolsets per role; sharpen overlapping boundaries; delete duplicate tools
rows.not: One mode-switch mega-tool or a routing paragraph in the prompt
rows.rule: Each added tool makes the others harder to choose between, so reduce and separate what each role sees instead of piling on wording.
rows.unless: Only two overlapping tools in a small, stable set. Sharpen those two descriptions first.

rows.signal: 'Just tell the agent never to call the delete tool'
rows.choose: Deny or remove the tool so the call cannot happen
rows.not: Bold system-prompt prohibition or a CLAUDE.md rule
rows.rule: An outcome that must hold every time is enforced by permissions or code. Instructions only make it more likely.

rows.signal: Every user's request runs through one admin service account
rows.choose: Act with the calling user's permissions; enforce authorization outside the model
rows.not: Keep the shared account and prompt the model to check roles
rows.rule: Enforce authorization outside the model, at the first point where the caller is known, and have the agent act with that caller's own permissions. A shared over-privileged account removes both the per-user boundary and the audit trail.
rows.unless: The data is non-sensitive and the same for every user (public docs). One low-privilege, read-only service identity is then fine.

rows.signal: Restricted documents retrieved, then redacted from the answer
rows.choose: Filter by entitlement before retrieval; keep secrets out of prompts entirely
rows.not: Post-generation redaction or an output filter as the control
rows.rule: Place the control before data crosses into the model. Redaction after generation acts once the exposure has already happened.

rows.signal: Our MCP server forwards the caller's token to downstream APIs
rows.choose: Validate audience; use separately scoped downstream credentials tied to the user
rows.not: Pass the incoming token straight through to downstream services
rows.rule: An MCP server accepts only tokens issued for it and never passes them through. Passthrough creates a confused deputy and bypasses downstream authorization.

rows.signal: Pipeline waits on full output; completion time misses target
rows.choose: Measure the dominant term first; then cut output, cache, or route tier
rows.not: Enable streaming to make it finish faster
rows.rule: Measure the dominant latency term before choosing a lever, and justify the choice against the accuracy floor. Streaming improves perceived latency, not completion time.
rows.unless: The complaint is a person watching and waiting. Streaming then fixes the perceived wait.

rows.signal: Most queries simple; tight p95 budget; accuracy floor non-negotiable
rows.choose: Route easy queries to a fast tier; escalate hard ones; verify floor per slice
rows.not: Largest tier for all traffic to protect accuracy
rows.rule: Justify tier and pipeline choices with measured accuracy against a p95-at-peak budget, and spend capability only where the hard slice needs it.
rows.unless: Query categories overlap so often that misroutes cost more than the latency saved.

rows.signal: Only request rate, errors and latency are captured; quality regressions go unseen
rows.choose: Instrument content traces: prompt and model versions, retrieved IDs, tool calls, outputs, correlation IDs
rows.not: More dashboards, alerts or a runbook on the same metrics
rows.rule: Instrument before you fix. Traces must capture prompt and model versions, retrieved context, tool calls and decision points under correlation IDs. Dashboards and runbooks only consume that telemetry.

rows.signal: Millions of requests daily; full payload capture too costly
rows.choose: Light record for every request; full traces for failures and flagged slices
rows.not: Uniform random sampling judged on one aggregate score
rows.rule: Sample so that failures and slices survive: every request gets a light correlated record, and heavy payloads are kept selectively by outcome and slice.

rows.signal: Answers miss exceptions; governing clause split across two chunks
rows.choose: Chunk on structural units; attach section headers or parent context
rows.not: Raise top-k, swap the embedding model, or add overlap as the only fix
rows.rule: Chunk by the corpus's own units and index for the query shape. Text cut at a chunk boundary is a content defect that needs a boundary fix, not more retrieval volume.
rows.unless: A unit runs longer than a chunk. A measured overlap (or parent-unit retrieval) then complements unit-boundary chunking; arbitrary overlap on its own never guarantees whole units.

rows.signal: One answer needs both policy wording and the claim's current status
rows.choose: Retrieve the wording; fetch status live from the system of record, then compose
rows.not: Index claim status alongside the documents and re-index often
rows.rule: Split by volatility: documents come from the index and live state from a system-of-record call at request time, combined in one answer.

rows.signal: Traffic mixes part numbers and error codes with conceptual questions
rows.choose: Hybrid retrieval: lexical for identifiers, semantic for concepts, routed by shape
rows.not: One dense index, or upgrade to a bigger model
rows.rule: Match retrieval to data shape and query pattern: exact identifiers go lexical, concepts go semantic, and mixed traffic is routed or hybrid.

rows.signal: Correct passage is in the candidate set but ranked low
rows.choose: Add a re-ranker over the retrieved candidates
rows.not: Raise top-k and pass more chunks to the model
rows.rule: High recall with low precision calls for re-ranking. More context volume adds noise, cost and latency.
rows.unless: The passage is missing from the candidates altogether: that is a recall or chunking defect, so fix it upstream. Or every passage above the cut-off is relevant and the question needs more passages than k (one per compared item): raise k to that count.

rows.signal: Results mix jurisdictions and superseded policy versions
rows.choose: Apply metadata filters (region, version, effective date) before semantic search
rows.not: Tell the model to ignore out-of-scope results
rows.rule: Narrow the search space with metadata filters before similarity search, instead of asking the model to discard noise after retrieval.

rows.signal: Three product surfaces need the same search capability
rows.choose: Build it once as an MCP server every client reuses
rows.not: Each team wires its own direct API integration
rows.rule: Choose the mechanism by reuse and reasoning: MCP for a capability several clients share at runtime, direct API/CLI for one app or a fixed pipeline, agent-to-agent only between independently reasoning systems, and a Skill for know-how that fetches nothing.
rows.unless: One app or a fixed pipeline you own end to end. A direct API/CLI call is simpler there.

rows.signal: Partner company's agent must negotiate terms with ours
rows.choose: Agent-to-agent: only task messages and results cross; each side keeps its tools, data stores and credentials
rows.not: Expose our internal MCP tools and credentials to their agent
rows.rule: Agent-to-agent fits independently reasoning systems that must fail independently. Only task messages and their results cross the boundary; each side's tools, internal data stores and credentials never do.
rows.unless: The remote side is a deterministic service with no independent reasoning. Call its API.

rows.signal: Hundreds of tools loaded up front; context bloated, selection degrading
rows.choose: Progressive discovery: expose metadata first, load full definitions on demand
rows.not: Truncate every description so the whole catalogue fits
rows.rule: For a large or growing catalogue, load capability details on demand (tool search, deferred loading, Skills that show metadata first and load the body on trigger). A small, stable toolset is fine loaded up front.
rows.unless: The catalogue is small and stable. Monolithic loading is then simpler and just as accurate.

rows.signal: Agent chains list_users, list_events and create_event for every booking; errors creep in
rows.choose: One typed workflow tool (schedule_event) that finds availability and books
rows.not: A routing paragraph, or one mode-switch tool spanning unrelated domains
rows.unless: Each step needs its own human approval or audit entry. Keep separate typed tools behind a workflow gate.
rows.rule: Design tools around the agent's task, not one per API endpoint: fold a chain of low-level calls into one typed workflow tool, and group operations on one resource behind an action parameter. A mode switch across unrelated domains is the trap.

rows.signal: Shared vector index across customers; the model supplies the tenant ID as a tool argument
rows.choose: Inject the tenant filter server-side from the authenticated session; per-tenant namespaces where contracts demand
rows.not: Instruct the model to always pass the caller's tenant ID
rows.rule: Tenant isolation is enforced by the server from the authenticated identity, never by an argument the model chooses; use separate namespaces or indexes where hard separation is contractual.

rows.signal: Research subagent can ask the payments agent to do anything the payments agent can
rows.choose: Per-agent identity; the receiver enforces a per-caller allowlist; delegated scope never exceeds the user's
rows.not: Tell the payments agent to refuse requests that seem out of scope
rows.unless: Both agents only read the same non-sensitive data. A shared low-privilege identity is then acceptable.
rows.rule: Authorize calls between internal agents like calls between services: each agent has its own identity, the receiver enforces what each caller may request, and delegated scope never exceeds the original user's.

rows.signal: Agent preloads hundreds of manuals into every request; accuracy and cost both suffer
rows.choose: Just-in-time: keep lightweight references; read documents through search or file tools when needed
rows.not: Load the whole knowledge base up front, or truncate every manual to fit
rows.unless: The corpus is small and stable, well under ~200k tokens and reused. Load it whole behind a cache breakpoint, with no RAG.
rows.rule: Apply progressive discovery to knowledge as well as tools: keep references in context and load documents on demand, unless the corpus is small and stable enough to cache whole.

rows.signal: Enterprise governs everything through its AWS account; a team plans a separate direct API contract
rows.choose: Pick the surface whose operator and controls fit: identity, billing, audit, residency, contract coverage
rows.not: Choose the surface with the newest features and bolt the controls on later
rows.unless: A required feature exists on only one surface. Confirm that surface meets the obligations before choosing it, and record the trade in an ADR.
rows.rule: Choose the deployment surface by who operates inference and whose identity, billing, audit, residency and contractual controls already govern it; then check feature and model parity and pin versions on that surface.

rows.signal: Team says 'accuracy looks good'; no target agreed
rows.choose: Pre-agree threshold, sample size and instrument per metric before building
rows.not: Ship on the observed score; set targets afterwards
rows.unless: No baseline exists yet. Measuring the current baseline is then the first step, and the threshold is set from it.
rows.rule: A number without a pre-agreed threshold is not an eval. Before you build, fix a threshold, a sample size and a measuring instrument for each of accuracy, latency, cost, safety and security.

rows.signal: Choose the latency metric for peak-hour customer chat
rows.choose: p95 at peak, with time-to-first-token and completion tracked separately
rows.not: One mean latency figure across the whole day
rows.unless: Offline or batch workload: commit to completion within the delivery window, not to per-request latency.
rows.rule: Define latency as tail percentiles at peak, split into time-to-first-token (what users feel) and completion (what callers wait on). A single daily mean hides the users who churn.

rows.signal: Agent can call write tools; pick safety and security metrics
rows.choose: Gate on unauthorized-action, injection-success and policy-violation rates using adversarial sets
rows.not: Fold safety into one blended quality score
rows.rule: Safety and security are separate gating metrics measured on adversarial and red-team slices (unauthorized actions, injection success, data leakage). Never average them into overall quality.

rows.signal: Mix of exact fields and free-text answers to grade
rows.choose: Code checks for crisp truth, calibrated rubric judge, experts for high stakes
rows.not: One LLM judge scores everything, exact fields included
rows.rule: Mixed methodology is a grading ladder: code or exact match where truth is crisp, a rubric LLM judge validated against human labels for open-ended quality, and expert review where stakes demand it. Run it on a held-out set drawn from real demand plus adversarial and edge slices, and kept out of prompt tuning. Gold labels and grades never come from the system under test; model-generated cases are fine as volume if seeded from and checked against real traffic. Prefer more automatically graded cases over a few hand-graded ones.

rows.signal: Judge scores climbing while customer complaints also rise
rows.choose: Recalibrate the judge against fresh human labels; re-check agreement
rows.not: Trust the judge; call it model drift
rows.rule: An LLM judge is an instrument that drifts. When its scores diverge from human outcomes, recalibrate it against fresh human labels before you trust any trend.

rows.signal: Offline eval steady, but errors rising in new region
rows.choose: Refresh the set from production traffic; add the region as a scored slice
rows.not: Trust the steady overall score and keep the old set
rows.rule: A steady aggregate on a stale set hides a failing slice. Refresh eval data from current traffic and score new segments separately.

rows.signal: 'Variant B is winning after 50 sessions; ship it?'
rows.choose: Hold to the pre-registered metric, sample size and stopping rule
rows.not: Stop early and declare the winner
rows.unless: A pre-declared guardrail metric (safety, severe errors) shows harm. Stopping early is then correct.
rows.rule: Lock the primary metric, guardrail metrics, sample size and stopping rule before the test starts, and change one thing per arm. Anything decided after peeking produces a false winner.

rows.signal: Variant bundles new prompt, new model and new retriever
rows.choose: One change per arm; offline eval first, then capped exposure with guardrails
rows.not: Test the bundle to save a cycle
rows.rule: Iterate one variable at a time. Pass the offline eval, then roll out to capped exposure with guardrail metrics that stop the rollout automatically.

rows.signal: After a doc refresh; model and latency unchanged
rows.choose: Check retrieval and indexing of the refreshed documents
rows.not: Model drift, temperature, or a shrunken context window
rows.rule: Diagnose the layer the triggering change touched, and use the 'unchanged' variables to rule out the rest. A document refresh points to ingestion, chunking and indexing, not to the model.

rows.signal: Correct passages retrieved, yet answer contradicts them
rows.choose: Treat as grounding failure: constrain to sources, cite, verify claims
rows.not: Raise top-k or re-index the corpus
rows.unless: Wrong passages retrieved (low recall@k): fix retrieval, not the prompt.
rows.rule: Evaluate retrieval separately from generation. Right documents with a wrong answer is a hallucination or grounding fault; wrong documents is a retrieval fault.

rows.signal: Fails equally on easy and hard items after prompt edit
rows.choose: Prompt failure: diff the prompt change and fix it against evals
rows.not: Upgrade to a larger model tier
rows.unless: Fails only on complex reasoning items: add step-by-step reasoning or higher effort for that slice first; if it still fails, it is a model mismatch, so route that slice up a tier, gated by evals.
rows.rule: Failure spread evenly across difficulty is a prompt problem. Failure concentrated in the hardest slice is a model-mismatch problem.

rows.signal: 'Cut cost per task'; no cost breakdown available
rows.choose: Measure the dominant term first: input, output, turns, retries per task
rows.not: Pull a favourite lever (cache, smaller tier) blind
rows.rule: Measure the dominant cost or latency term per completed task before you choose a lever. Caching helps only repeated input, batching helps only non-interactive work, and streaming improves only perceived latency.

rows.signal: Overnight reports; accuracy floor fixed; reduce cost
rows.choose: Batch the non-interactive jobs and cache the stable prefix
rows.not: Trim context or downsize tier regardless of fit
rows.unless: If a user waits on the result, keep it synchronous; cache and right-size output instead.
rows.rule: Under an accuracy commitment, prefer levers that leave what the model reads unchanged (batching, caching) over trimming context or downgrading the tier.

rows.signal: Nothing was deployed, but answer quality dropped
rows.choose: Pull traces of failing vs passing requests: prompts, retrievals, tool results
rows.not: Roll back, fail over, or build a dashboard first
rows.rule: Observe before you change anything. Diagnose a quality regression from the content of the failing requests (prompts, retrieved context, tool calls, outputs), tied to version and correlation IDs. Rate, error and latency metrics look the same before and after, and dashboards or runbooks only consume that instrumentation.

rows.signal: Need debug logs, but prompts contain customer PII
rows.choose: Redact at capture; light record per session, access-controlled heavy payloads
rows.not: Log raw prompts; redact later in the warehouse
rows.rule: Log a light record for every session, with version and correlation IDs, and minimise PII at the point of capture. Sampling away sessions or keeping only errors deletes the evidence you will need later.

rows.signal: The current model's retirement date is announced; the team plans to switch the model ID on Friday
rows.choose: Pin versions; re-tune the prompt for the replacement, run the full regression suite, then a capped rollout
rows.not: Swap the model ID and watch complaints
rows.rule: Pin a specific model version and treat every model change as a release: re-tune the prompt for the new model, pass the full regression suite with the migration as the one change, then widen from capped exposure, all before the retirement date.

rows.signal: Prompt tweaks ship straight to production after a few spot checks
rows.choose: Standing regression suite in CI on every prompt, model, tool or index change; the full suite gates release
rows.not: Spot-check a handful of favourite examples before each release
rows.unless: The full suite is slow. Run a fast regression subset per change and the full suite before release.
rows.rule: Every prompt, model, tool or index change reruns a standing regression suite in CI, with past failures locked in as cases, and the full held-out suite gates the release.

rows.signal: Replacing a rules engine; no production labels; customer-facing errors unacceptable
rows.choose: Shadow mode on live traffic; compare with incumbent decisions; widen segment by segment by agreement
rows.not: Switch all traffic over once the offline eval passes
rows.unless: The change is low-risk and reversible behind a flag. A small canary with rollback criteria is then enough.
rows.rule: Name the rollout stage by its question: shadow mode compares on live traffic without serving, a canary checks for harm against the baseline, and an A/B test picks the better variant. Each widens only through gates set in advance.

rows.signal: Quality dropped right after Tuesday's prompt release; one slice is failing
rows.choose: Roll back behind the flag to the known-good version; diff before and after traces for that slice
rows.not: Call it model drift and switch model tier
rows.unless: Nothing was deployed. Then pull failing and passing traces first (CS-D4-14); there is no known-good state to return to.
rows.rule: When a regression follows a known change, a known-good version exists: contain by rolling back the change, then compare traces from before and after on the failing slice.

rows.signal: On-call is paged for every cost blip and thumbs-down; real incidents get ignored
rows.choose: Page only on sustained user-impacting symptoms (SLO burn); route trends to an owned review queue
rows.not: Add more alerts and dashboards on the same signals
rows.rule: Page a named owner only on sustained, user-impacting symptoms; send trends and single signals to a review queue, and add leading indicators such as retrieval relevance and abstention rate.

rows.signal: Agent eval fails runs that reached the right end state by a different tool sequence
rows.choose: Grade the outcome and end state; keep trajectory metrics as diagnostics
rows.not: Require an exact match to one golden tool-call sequence
rows.unless: The path itself is the requirement (a mandated approval step, a forbidden tool). Check that step explicitly as well.
rows.rule: Grade agents on outcomes and end state, not one exact trajectory; use trajectory metrics to diagnose, and check mandated steps explicitly.

rows.signal: The model and prompt that wrote the answers also grade them
rows.choose: Separate judge context, different model or version, specific rubric, reasoning before a constrained verdict
rows.not: Have the generating model rate its own answers at temperature 0
rows.rule: Keep the judge independent of the generator: its own context without the generator's rationale, preferably a different, pinned model or version, a specific rubric and reasoning before a constrained verdict.

rows.signal: One shared API key serves five use cases; finance cannot see which drives spend
rows.choose: A workspace per use case: its own spend and rate limits, with usage and cost reported per workspace
rows.not: Cut every team's usage by the same percentage
rows.rule: Give each use case its own workspace so that spend limits, rate limits and usage and cost reporting attribute to it (a separate API key attributes usage only), then optimise the dominant consumer.

rows.signal: Guardrail layer times out; the agent proceeds with the action unchecked
rows.choose: Fail closed: block the action until the outside-the-model control answers
rows.not: Fail open for availability and alert on the gap afterwards
rows.rule: A guarantee needs a control point outside the model that can refuse the action and that fails closed when a layer errors. A prompt only raises the odds that the model complies.
rows.unless: The action is low-risk and reversible and the stem puts availability first. Failing open with alerting can then be acceptable.

rows.signal: Assistant holds a tool the use case never needs
rows.choose: Remove the capability; screening cannot block what the role permits
rows.not: Output screening, confirmation prompt, or audit log around it
rows.rule: When the role never needs a capability, remove it. Filters, confirmations and logs are compensating controls on a risk you chose to keep.
rows.unless: The role genuinely needs the action; then keep it, scope it narrowly and gate it by risk

rows.signal: Select TWO: stop the leak and know if it happens
rows.choose: Pair one preventive control with one detective control
rows.not: Monitoring or alerting offered as the preventive control
rows.rule: Match the control type to the ask. Prevention stops the damage and detection tells you it happened; neither substitutes for the other.
rows.unless: The stem asks only how anyone would find out; then the detective control is the answer. If it asks only for prevention ('never reach customers'), two complementary preventive layers, such as a policy guardrail plus a workflow-enforced approval before sending, are the pair

rows.signal: Agent reads external emails or web pages and can send outbound
rows.choose: Treat fetched text as data; strip its authority and bound outbound reach
rows.not: Tell the model to ignore embedded instructions; use bigger model
rows.rule: Prompt injection is bounded, not solved. Lower the authority that untrusted content carries and limit what a successful injection can reach. Exfiltration needs both an instruction channel and an outbound path, so cutting either one breaks it.
rows.unless: Labelling and delimiting fetched content and stating an untrusted-content policy is a sound first layer. It complements removing authority and bounding outbound reach; it never replaces them.

rows.signal: Before pilot, sponsor asks you to guarantee no hallucinations
rows.choose: Failure-mode register: each mode, independent check, fallback, residual risk, owner
rows.not: Promise zero errors or quote the demo's accuracy
rows.rule: Name the failure modes and the residual risk honestly. Catch confident errors with verification that does not depend on the model, and define a fallback for when a dependency fails.

rows.signal: 'The model reports 95% confidence, so auto-approve it'
rows.choose: Route by reversibility, blast radius and cost using calibrated system signals
rows.not: Escalation threshold on model self-reported confidence
rows.rule: Route human review by reversibility, blast radius and the cost of an error, using calibrated signals from the system. Never route by the model's self-reported confidence.
rows.unless: A separate classifier's score, calibrated against labelled outcomes, can be one routing input alongside risk rules. The model's own self-rating never is.

rows.signal: Reviewers approve nearly every draft unedited within seconds
rows.choose: Treat the gate as failed: risk-target the queue, surface evidence, audit reviewers
rows.not: Keep 100% review, or add reviewers to the same queue
rows.rule: Near-total unedited approval in seconds is automation bias: the human gate exists only on paper and has to be redesigned, not staffed up.
rows.unless: Volume is low and every item is high-stakes, as in an early pilot. Keep full review, but give reviewers the evidence and track override rates.

rows.signal: Small external refund email vs large internal reversible reclassification
rows.choose: Gate the small irreversible external action; sample the reversible internal one
rows.not: Gate by transaction size, clock window, or random 10%
rows.rule: A small action that is irreversible and visible outside the company outranks a large reversible internal one. Put the synchronous gate on it and use risk-weighted sampling for the high-volume, low-severity work.

rows.signal: Clinical notes containing PHI will be sent to the model
rows.choose: BAA with the party operating inference (Anthropic on the Claude API; AWS or Google on Bedrock or Vertex AI), HIPAA-eligible configuration, audit logging; send only the minimum necessary PHI
rows.not: Zero data retention alone, or 'model, ignore the PHI'
rows.rule: Enforce compliance before data crosses the boundary, using the mechanism the regime actually requires: for HIPAA a BAA plus eligible configuration plus audit logging, for GDPR minimisation, for FedRAMP an authorised environment. Map each obligation to a named control, an owner and an evidence artefact.
rows.unless: If the data is properly de-identified before the call, it is no longer PHI and the BAA question falls away. ZDR changes retention only and never substitutes for the BAA.

rows.signal: EU shop injects full customer profiles into every prompt
rows.choose: Minimise: send only the fields this request needs
rows.not: Encrypt it, pseudonymise the name, or collect consent
rows.rule: GDPR minimisation means less personal data arrives in the first place. Encryption, consent and pseudonymising a single field protect the data or legitimise its use, but they do not shrink the payload.

rows.signal: Select TWO: federal or in-region obligation; auditor wants proof
rows.choose: Authorised in-region deployment plus tamper-evident evidence record with named owner
rows.not: Vendor SOC 2 letter, a DPA, or logging everything forever
rows.rule: A residency or authorisation obligation is met by where and how the workload runs, and it is proven by an evidence artefact someone owns. Residency needs a geography-bound endpoint and every store on the data path (vector store, prompt and response logs, traces, error tracker, backups, subprocessors) in-region. A vendor's attestations are not your compliance.

rows.signal: Overall accuracy strong; one applicant group's denial errors rising
rows.choose: Measure outcomes per subgroup against pre-agreed disparity thresholds
rows.not: Cite the aggregate, or 'no protected attribute in inputs'
rows.rule: Prove fairness by testing outcomes for each group against thresholds agreed in advance, not with the aggregate score or the input schema. The accountable business owner decides the resulting trade-off and documents it; the architect does not.

rows.signal: Customers unaware they chat with AI; transparency now required
rows.choose: Disclose AI in context, with an escalation path to a human
rows.not: A terms-of-service line, or exposing raw chain of thought
rows.rule: Transparency means the user sees the disclosure at the point of interaction and has a way to reach a human. A policy page only makes the information available, and raw reasoning traces do not explain the decision.

rows.signal: New content screen blocks 15% of legitimate requests; support tickets surge
rows.choose: Measure false-positive and false-negative rates on labelled sets; set the threshold by relative harm; offer a route onward
rows.not: Keep the strict threshold, since blocking more is always safer
rows.unless: The blocked category must never get through (for example, regulated data leaving). Keep the block and fix false positives with a better check, not a looser threshold.
rows.rule: Calibrate a guardrail on labelled data for both over-blocking and misses, choose its operating point by the relative harm of each, and give blocked users a clear decline and a route onward.

rows.signal: Automated loan denials; accuracy is excellent and the team wants to drop human review
rows.choose: Keep the mandated human decision: GDPR solely-automated rules, EU AI Act high-risk duties, Usage Policy review
rows.not: Drop review because measured accuracy exceeds the bar
rows.unless: No law or policy mandates review and the decision is low-stakes and reversible. Then route by consequence as usual.
rows.rule: Where law or the Usage Policy mandates human oversight of a decision (solely automated significant decisions, high-risk AI uses), the review gate is a requirement, not a design choice weighed against accuracy.

rows.signal: A customer requests erasure; their data sits in logs, a vector index and last month's eval set
rows.choose: Trace lineage to every derived store; delete or re-index each, keeping only what a legal duty requires
rows.not: Delete the source record and let the copies age out
rows.rule: Data-subject rights reach every derived copy: logs, traces, caches, indexes, memory and eval sets. Build lineage in so that requests can be honoured, and retain only what a specific legal duty covers.

rows.signal: Board asks whether the model vendor is responsible for wrongful automated denials
rows.choose: Deployer is accountable: a named owner accepts residual risk; intended use, limits and versions documented
rows.not: Point to the vendor's model card and contract as the responsible party
rows.rule: Accountability for automated decisions stays with the deploying organisation and a named owner who accepts residual risk; vendor documents are evidence about the vendor, not a transfer of responsibility.

rows.signal: Discovery 'done' after one sponsor workshop; users and data owners never consulted
rows.choose: Finish discovery: user-sourced baseline, measurable target, constraint inventory, named owner
rows.not: Start design from the sponsor's wish list
rows.rule: Discovery is finished only when a current-process baseline, a measurable target, a constraint inventory and a named decision owner are agreed. Anything built before then answers a question nobody has asked yet.
rows.unless: The stem says these are already agreed and asks for the next step. Then move to design.

rows.signal: Sponsor asks for X, but call logs show the pain is Y
rows.choose: Bring the underlying-job evidence to the sponsor and reframe with them
rows.not: Build the literal ask, or quietly build your own version
rows.rule: Design against the underlying job, not the literal ask. When the two differ, the sponsor makes the reframe from your evidence; you do not make it for them.

rows.signal: Kickoff for a regulated workflow; data access and residency unknown
rows.choose: Map data, access and constraints (residency, compliance, latency, cost) first
rows.not: Shortlist and benchmark models on sample prompts
rows.rule: Ask the discovery question that surfaces the hidden binding constraint (residency, compliance, data access) before you choose any model or design.

rows.signal: Executive insists on 99.9% accuracy before approving
rows.choose: Convert to error counts by case type; offer trade-off curve with HITL
rows.not: Promise 99.9%, refuse outright, or quietly redefine accuracy
rows.rule: Present a trade-off as a bounded choice the owner can act on. Turn percentages into error counts by case type, set cost and risk against the cost of reversing the decision, and put human review on the high-stakes slice. Never promise the number, refuse it, or quietly redefine it.

rows.signal: Ten-minute board slot to approve the architecture
rows.choose: Lead with decision and business impact, then risks, mitigations, the ask
rows.not: Walk through architecture diagram, chunking and prompt design
rows.rule: Executives get the decision and its business impact in metrics they already track, then the key risks with their mitigations, then the specific ask. Give them no implementation detail.
rows.unless: The audience is the engineering team taking over the build. Then implementation detail is the right artefact.

rows.signal: Pilot misses the agreed accuracy bar; select TWO
rows.choose: Report segmented results with method; give owner bounded options and costs
rows.not: Lower the bar yourself or cancel the project unilaterally
rows.rule: When the evidence misses or contradicts an agreed bar, take the segmented evidence and bounded options to the decision owner. Do not accept or abandon the bar on their behalf.

rows.signal: SLA draft says 'average latency' and excludes peak season
rows.choose: p95 at peak, accuracy floor on agreed eval set, error budget, remedy
rows.not: Averages, surge-day exclusions, or hard per-request max
rows.rule: An SLA for a probabilistic system commits to percentile latency measured at peak, an accuracy floor on an agreed eval set with an error budget, cost per transaction, and a remedy. It never commits to deterministic correctness.
rows.unless: A hard per-request timeout is fine as an internal engineering guard, just not as the contractual SLA for generative work.

rows.signal: Sales told the client 'it never gets answers wrong'
rows.choose: Reset expectations now: probabilistic output, measured quality, review path, remedy
rows.not: Tune prompts quietly and hope complaints stay low
rows.rule: Set probabilistic expectations early and in writing: measured quality, a review path for the failures, and a remedy. Silence after an overpromise turns into a trust failure later.

rows.signal: User thumbs-downs pile up on a dashboard nobody acts on
rows.choose: Set review triggers and a named owner; feed failures into the eval set
rows.not: Add satisfaction charts and ask users to rate more
rows.rule: A feedback loop is closed only when it has pre-agreed review triggers, a named owner who must act, and a path that turns real failures into eval cases. A dashboard on its own is an open loop.

rows.signal: 'In a year, how will anyone know why we chose this?'
rows.choose: Version-controlled ADR: context, options, decision, consequences, rejected alternatives, revisit trigger
rows.not: Code comments, a meeting recording, or the system prompt
rows.rule: To preserve the reasoning, write a version-controlled ADR that records context, the options considered, the decision, its consequences, why each alternative was rejected and the condition that would reopen it. Code comments, recordings and prompts lose the 'why'.

rows.signal: Ops takes over Monday; 'just ping us in the channel'
rows.choose: Handoff pack: runbooks, eval suite, prompt inventory, known limitations, escalation paths, named owner
rows.not: A chat channel or architect contact as the documentation
rows.rule: A handoff must survive your absence. Transfer runbooks (symptom, cause, action), the eval suite, the prompt inventory, known limitations with their escalation paths and diagnostic access to a named owner, then coach them through the first incident instead of staying the permanent fixer.

rows.signal: POC demo impressed, no exit criteria, sponsor wants production
rows.choose: Run a pilot on pre-agreed exit criteria; production adds SLOs, rollback
rows.not: Promote the POC or extend the pilot unchanged
rows.rule: Each lifecycle stage has its own exit gate. A POC proves feasibility, a pilot proves value against pre-agreed criteria, and production adds SLOs, on-call, rollback and a named owner. Nothing moves up without passing its gate.
rows.unless: A pilot failed with no criteria set. Then define the criteria with the owner before retrying; do not simply rerun it.

rows.signal: Months after handoff, complaints rise and nobody owns monitoring
rows.choose: Name a monitoring owner; pull traces and slice evals before changing anything
rows.not: Swap the model or re-architect before diagnosing
rows.rule: Monitoring after handoff needs a named owner. Iteration starts from traces and per-slice evals, and the evidence decides whether you iterate or re-architect.
rows.unless: The diagnosis shows the use case, data or regulatory regime has changed. Then re-architect instead of iterating.

rows.signal: Regulated customer data in scope; discovery attendees are the sponsor and engineering only
rows.choose: Bring legal, security, privacy or compliance and the data owners into discovery before design
rows.not: Start design and send legal the finished architecture for sign-off
rows.unless: The data is public and non-sensitive. The core roles in CS-D6-01 then suffice.
rows.rule: When regulated or sensitive data is in scope, legal, security and privacy or compliance join discovery with the data owners, because they hold the constraints that eliminate designs.

rows.signal: Two department heads want opposite operating points; neither has authority over the other
rows.choose: Show the measured trade-off with your recommendation; one accountable owner (else the sponsor) decides; record it
rows.not: Split the difference yourself or build both variants
rows.rule: When peers disagree, present the measured trade-off and your recommendation with its reversal condition, get one accountable owner to decide (the sponsor if none exists), and record the decision.

rows.signal: Mid-build, a VP asks to add two document types 'while you're at it'
rows.choose: Impact analysis against the baseline; the sponsor decides; formally re-baseline scope, date and eval set
rows.not: Absorb it quietly, or refuse outright because scope is frozen
rows.unless: The change is within delegated authority and moves no cost, date or risk the sponsor can see.
rows.rule: Every new requirement gets an impact assessment against the agreed baseline; the sponsor decides, and an accepted change is re-baselined and passes through design and the eval gate.

rows.signal: Pilot on one team hit every exit criterion; the sponsor wants an org-wide rollout next month
rows.choose: Re-check pilot assumptions at scale (input mix, edge-case rate, support load, cost at volume) before widening
rows.not: Roll out everywhere on the pilot's numbers
rows.unless: The pilot population already represents the full traffic mix and volume. Proceed through the production readiness gate.
rows.rule: Before scaling a pilot, re-check its assumptions against production: input distribution, edge-case frequency, support load and cost at volume.

rows.signal: 'Must not be disableable on any developer machine'
rows.choose: Managed settings `permissions.deny`, enforced by the client above every lower scope
rows.not: Committed project settings rolled out repo by repo
rows.rule: Choose the scope by the reach and overridability you need: org-wide and non-overridable means managed settings, team-shared means committed project config, personal means user config.
rows.unless: If the org-wide need is guidance (coding standards), not enforcement, use managed CLAUDE.md instead.

rows.signal: 'Team Claude Code setups have drifted; new hires miss conventions'
rows.choose: Commit CLAUDE.md, project settings and `.mcp.json` with `${ENV_VAR}` secrets
rows.not: Ask each developer to copy it into user config
rows.rule: Team-wide behaviour belongs in version-controlled project config. User-level config never propagates, and secrets never go into committed files.
rows.unless: Personal preferences and experimental servers correctly stay in user scope.

rows.signal: 'PHI scrub or secrets-path ban lives only in CLAUDE.md'
rows.choose: Fail-closed PreToolUse hook plus a deny rule on the sensitive path
rows.not: Rewrite CLAUDE.md in stronger, bolded wording
rows.rule: CLAUDE.md and memory files are advisory context. Anything that must happen every time needs a protected, fail-closed hook or permission rule.

rows.signal: 'Leadership asks whether the coding-assistant rollout actually worked'
rows.choose: Before/after outcomes (cycle time, escaped defects) vs pre-agreed baseline, plus mechanism
rows.not: Seats activated, usage hours or accepted lines of code
rows.rule: Prove enablement with outcomes measured against a baseline and threshold agreed before rollout, plus the mechanism that moved them. Seats, usage and accepted lines are input measures.
rows.unless: If no baseline was ever captured, the FIRST step is to capture one before expanding the rollout.

rows.signal: 'Unattended CI review job only posts comments, yet can push'
rows.choose: Headless run that loads only explicit config; allowlist read and comment tools only
rows.not: Keep push access but log and alert on pushes
rows.rule: Headless CI runs get a protected, non-interactive policy with an explicit minimal allowlist. Remove capabilities the job never needs instead of monitoring them.

rows.signal: 'Speed up code review without lowering the quality bar'
rows.choose: Independent AI first-pass review before humans; humans keep the merge decision
rows.not: Coding agent self-reviews and auto-merges its own changes
rows.rule: Put AI on an enumerable, toil-heavy step such as first-pass review or fixed CI checks. Use a reviewer instance independent of the author and keep the human decision intact.
rows.unless: Low-risk, fully test-gated change classes may auto-merge if the policy owner explicitly approves it.

rows.signal: 'Project MCP server fails for one team; others fine'
rows.choose: FIRST inspect what loaded for that team: approval state, env vars, logs
rows.not: Widen its permissions, reinstall, or fail over immediately
rows.rule: Observe before you change anything: pull traces, logs and the config that actually loaded for the failing slice before you widen access, restart or fail over. Silent failures (a dismissed approval, a misspelled hook matcher) show up only there.

rows.signal: 'Tools denied since the managed-settings rollout; repo code unchanged'
rows.choose: Trace scope precedence; the managed rule outranks every lower scope
rows.not: Add allow rules in project or user settings
rows.rule: Settings resolve managed > CLI args > project local > shared project > user. Nothing below can override a managed deny, so take the fix to the owner of the managed policy.
rows.unless: If no managed rule matches, look for a deny at any other scope. Deny beats allow across every scope.

rows.signal: Agentic coding results are poor in a legacy repo with no tests; changes 'look done' but break
rows.choose: Give Claude a check it can run (tests, build, lint named in CLAUDE.md); add characterisation tests first
rows.not: Switch to a larger model or write longer CLAUDE.md guidance
rows.rule: Agentic coding needs a verification loop: a test, build, lint or screenshot check that Claude can run and read. Where tests are missing, add them first, and confirm generated tests fail against broken code.

rows.signal: Forty repos each carry a copied review skill and commands; versions drift
rows.choose: Package them as a versioned plugin in an org marketplace; named owner, reviewed changes, staged rollout
rows.not: Copy the latest files into every repo again, or ask developers to install them personally
rows.unless: The requirement is enforcement, not shared know-how. Use managed settings (CS-D7-01).
rows.rule: Distribute shared skills, commands and hooks across many repositories as a versioned plugin from an organisation marketplace, owned and reviewed like code and rolled out in stages.

rows.signal: API keys are exported as shell variables on machines running Claude Code
rows.choose: Credential helper or secret manager; deny reads of .env and secrets paths; sandbox untrusted repos
rows.not: Tell Claude in CLAUDE.md never to print environment variables
rows.rule: Assume the agent can read whatever its shell can: fetch credentials through a helper or secret manager, deny secret paths (Read deny rules cover Claude's file tools and recognised shell file commands, not arbitrary scripts), use sandbox filesystem restrictions where the block must hold, and isolate untrusted repositories in a VM or a sandbox with filesystem and network isolation (the docs recommend dev containers for trusted repositories only).

rows.signal: Production incident; an engineer wants Claude Code to find the cause and push the fix
rows.choose: Claude triages logs, traces and change events and narrows hypotheses; a human approves the production fix
rows.not: Let the agent apply its fix to production directly
rows.unless: The fix is a pre-approved, reversible runbook action. Automation may run it within that runbook's bounds.
rows.rule: Use Claude to investigate incidents (logs, traces, change correlation, hypotheses) but keep a human approving production changes, and check AI-drafted incident records against the evidence.

1.what_it_rewards: Picking the simplest pattern and component split that meets the stem's binding business constraint. That means discovery comes first, the feedback loop is closed, and value is claimed on the right denominator.
remember3: Choose the simplest pattern that works: augmented call, then workflow, then agent, then multi-agent. Move up only when steps emerge at runtime and errors are recoverable (for an agent), or when the work is truly independent (for multiple agents). Difficulty and org charts never justify the next step up.

Discovery comes before design, and a closed loop comes after it. Agree baseline, target, constraints and owner first. No design is end-to-end until real outcomes flow back to a named owner who acts on them.

Keep deterministic what must be deterministic. Facts, calculations, entitlements, live state and regulated controls belong in code or the system of record. Claude handles judgement over unstructured input.
1.foundations_delta: Carried over from CCAR-F: the pattern ladder, hub-and-spoke orchestration, explicit context in subagent handoffs, and chaining vs parallel decomposition. Now low-yield: Agent-tool (formerly Task) and allowedTools mechanics, stop_reason loops and SDK wiring, because orchestration shrank from a 27% domain to two objectives inside a 17% one. New at Professional: discovery-first framing; feedback loops that reach a named owner; the delegation boundary between Claude, deterministic systems and humans; and aligning value claims and SLAs to the right pillar.

2.what_it_rewards: Matching the lever to the defect: the cheapest tier that clears a measured bar, the prompting technique that fits the failure type, less context rather than more, and structural reuse (a stable prefix that gets cached, versioned Skills). A prompt never stands in for enforcement.
remember3: Stable content first, changing content last, then cache. It is the one lever that cuts both time-to-first-token and input cost without dropping required context (official Sample 2). Any change early in the prefix wipes out cache hits, and caching changes price, not how much of the window is used.

Match the fix to the failure. Few-shot fixes format and tone, step-by-step reasoning or more effort fixes multi-step logic, and a higher tier is justified only when failures come down to reasoning depth. Otherwise use the cheapest tier that clears a measured bar, with routing.

A prompt is not a guarantee, and more context is not better. Rules that must always hold are enforced in code outside the model. When cost and recall get worse together, reduce what enters the window rather than enlarging, reordering or adding emphasis.
2.foundations_delta: These carry over from CCAR-F: few-shot for format versus chain-of-thought for reasoning, prompt versus programmatic enforcement, and stable-first ordering for caching. Low-yield at Professional level: parameter names, cache TTLs and price multipliers, effort-level names, stop reasons and Batch limits, since items rarely turn on API mechanics. New emphasis: tier choice under cost, latency and eval evidence (routing, and the counter-trap where a higher tier is right). Also new: why caching and restructuring beat truncation or downsizing, when to compact, clear or filter context, and treating Skills and prompt modules as versioned artefacts with an owner and eval gates, versus MCP for reaching live systems.

3.what_it_rewards: Putting each concern at the layer that owns it: remove capability, authorize outside the model, fix retrieval where the defect actually is, choose the lightest mechanism that fits reuse, and read traces before you change anything.
remember3: Remove, don't guard. Least privilege deletes a capability the role does not need. Authorization lives outside the model and uses the caller's own permissions: no shared service account, no token passthrough, no post-hoc redaction.

Fix retrieval at the layer that is broken. Use unit-boundary chunking for split clauses, lexical, semantic or hybrid retrieval by query shape, re-ranking for precision, filters before search, and the system of record for live state. Widen k only for a measured recall gap, never for noisy results or split units, and never reach for a bigger model.

Choose the mechanism by reuse and reasoning: MCP for a shared capability, direct API/CLI for a one-off, agent-to-agent for independent reasoners. Use progressive discovery for large catalogues and pull traces before any fix.
3.foundations_delta: Tool scoping per role, least privilege, basic MCP-versus-direct-integration choices and "a prompt is not enforcement" all carry over from CCAR-F. The mechanics are low-yield at Professional level: `.mcp.json` scopes, `isError` payload fields, `tool_choice` values and env-var substitution. Foundations' "sharpen the tool description first" still wins for two overlapping tools, but at catalogue scale the answer moves to role scoping and progressive discovery. New and high-yield: RAG chunking, indexing and retrieval matched to query shape; MCP authentication (audience validation, no passthrough, per-user identity); observability and sampling at scale; accuracy-latency trade-offs justified against a p95 budget; and agent-to-agent as a third integration option.

4.what_it_rewards: Evidence over intuition: agree thresholds before building, use calibrated instruments, score every slice, run disciplined experiments, and diagnose the layer the change touched before you pull any lever.
remember3: A number is an eval only if it has a pre-agreed threshold, a calibrated instrument and per-slice scoring. Judges and eval sets drift like any other component.
Diagnose the layer the triggering change touched, and use the 'unchanged' variables to eliminate options. Pull the failing requests' traces before you fix anything.
Measure the dominant cost or latency term before you choose a lever. Under an accuracy floor, batch and cache rather than trim context or downsize the tier.
4.foundations_delta: CCAR-F touched evaluation mostly through mechanics: few-shot for consistency, schema validation, retry-with-feedback, and Message Batches limits and custom_id. What carries over is the idea that valid syntax is not semantic correctness, and that batching is for non-interactive work. New at Professional level: evals as acceptance criteria (thresholds, datasets drawn from real demand, a grading ladder, judge calibration), A/B discipline, diagnosing by layer, cost-per-task optimisation, and observability under PII constraints. Low-yield here: Batch API field names and window arithmetic, stop_reason handling, and exact prices or cache multipliers.

5.what_it_rewards: Picking the control that actually stops the harm, placed outside the model and before the data boundary, with human review routed by stakes and honest, per-group evidence handed to a named owner. The reassuring option and the "tell the model to" option both lose.
remember3: Ask what physically stops the action if the model does exactly the wrong thing. The answer should be a control outside the model that fails closed. Remove capabilities the role never needs, and remember that detection is never prevention.

Route humans by reversibility, blast radius and the cost of an error, never by the model's self-reported confidence. Reviewers who approve nearly everything unedited in seconds mean the gate exists only on paper.

Compliance is binary and sits upstream. A legal objection gates the option and is not weighed against cost. ZDR is not HIPAA. Minimisation means less data arrives. Fairness is measured per group, and a named business owner accepts the residual risk.
5.foundations_delta: Carried over from CCAR-F: programmatic enforcement over prompt instructions for critical rules, no escalation on self-reported confidence or sentiment, and aggregate accuracy hiding per-type failures. New at Professional level: mapping regulations (GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP) to a control, an owner and an evidence artefact; containing prompt injection; spotting rubber-stamped human gates; fairness and transparency; and leaving risk acceptance to the business owner. Low-yield: hook syntax, escalation-trigger mechanics and platform-specific residency parameters or price multipliers. Those belong in volatile platform facts, not in the rules.

6.what_it_rewards: The honest, segmented, defensible stakeholder action at the right lifecycle stage, with the decision left to its owner, rather than the reassuring or technically clever answer.
remember3: Stage first. Find the lifecycle stage in the stem: no baseline, target, constraints or owner means the answer is discovery. POC, pilot and production each have their own exit gate.
Don't overpromise and don't decide for the stakeholder. Turn accuracy targets into error counts and trade-offs, then bring segmented evidence and bounded options to the decision owner.

Match the artefact to the audience and the purpose. Executives get decision, impact, risk and the ask. Recorded reasoning goes in an ADR. A handoff pack goes to a named owner, never to a chat channel. SLAs are p95 at peak plus an accuracy floor, error budget and remedy.
6.foundations_delta: None of this domain carries over from CCAR-F. It is Professional-only, and Foundations mechanics (tool_choice, CLAUDE.md hierarchy, stop_reason loops) are low-yield here. The only thing that carries over is the habit of finding the binding constraint. New at Professional level: discovery outputs, exec-versus-engineer communication, SLAs for probabilistic systems (percentiles at peak, error budgets, remedies), ADRs and handoff packages, and POC/pilot/production exit gates. Technically strong candidates lose the most points here, because the right answer is often a stakeholder action rather than a technical fix.

7.what_it_rewards: Placing each Claude Code control at the scope and mechanism that actually guarantees it, then showing or debugging enablement with evidence (outcomes against a baseline, traces, loaded config) instead of activity counts or guesswork.
remember3: Scope is reach times overridability. If it cannot be disabled on any machine, use managed settings. If it is team-shared, use committed project config. User config is for personal use only and never propagates.
CLAUDE.md guides and does not enforce. Guarantees come from fail-closed hooks, deny rules and explicit tool allowlists, and headless CI runs need them too.
Evidence before action. Pull traces and the loaded config before you widen access or fail over, and judge a rollout by outcomes against a baseline, not by seats or accepted lines.
7.foundations_delta: Carries over from CCAR-F: CLAUDE.md and the project-vs-user config split, a committed `.mcp.json` with env-var secrets, hooks over prompts for guarantees, and headless `-p` runs. At about 4 CCAR-P items, learn the decision (which scope, which enforcement point) rather than the syntax. Low-yield here: @import depth, `.claude/rules` glob syntax, skill frontmatter keys, output-format flags, stop_reason loops. New at Professional level: managed settings as the org-wide non-overridable layer (managed CLAUDE.md is for guidance only), precedence-based diagnosis of denials after a rollout, adoption measured as outcomes against a baseline, and observe-before-change operational debugging.
